Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01162
Historical sources tell us that Maʿbad went to the Hijaz carrying his Qadarite message to a region whose people were generally more conservative in religious matters than the people of Iraq.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01163
There he met the scholars of Medina and explained his doctrine to them. The scholars of Medina were known for being among the strictest Muslim scholars on questions of religion and belief.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01164
What response did Maʿbad find among them?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01165

One of the great historians of Islamic beliefs gives us the answer. He was himself a major Sunni scholar and an opponent of Qadarite doctrine, yet he openly admits how widely the doctrine had spread at that time.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01166
Speaking specifically about the Qadarites, he says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01167

“…and among those who escaped these false doctrines, there remained only a small group from among the most distinguished scholars and the righteous early generations whom God protected from deviation and error…”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01168

He says this because the historical record tells us that Maʿbad influenced the scholars of Medina, who adopted his doctrine, just as he influenced many people in Iraq, a region strongly hostile to the Umayyads.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01169
This historical reality shows very clearly that the Qadarite idea could appeal even to conservative religious scholars who held great influence over public opinion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01170
So we have to ask: what was it about Qadarite doctrine that attracted these scholars and so many other people?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01171
Was it simply the “philosophical necessity of the human mind”?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01172
Was it simply an attempt to reconcile passages in the Qurʾān?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01173

Or was it simply the result of Christian theological influence transmitted through the man said to have been called Sansawayh, or Sawsan as Ibn Qutayba calls him in al-Maʿārif, and who is also mentioned in Mīzān al-Iʿtidāl? He was said to have been a Christian, then to have converted to Islam, then returned to Christianity, and to have influenced Maʿbad al-Juhanī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01174
If “philosophical necessity” alone explains the doctrine, why did this necessity appear at this particular moment rather than before or after it?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01175
Why did this particular side of the attempt to reconcile Qurʾānic passages—the side supporting human freedom—appeal to so many people in Iraq and the Hijaz, and later in Damascus?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01176
By contrast, the doctrine of compulsion first appeared through Jahm ibn Ṣafwān in Tirmidh, in the region of Marw in Persia, and through al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Najjār in Rayy, also in Persia.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01177

Why, then, did Qadarite doctrine flourish in Arab regions closely connected, directly or indirectly, to the political struggle between the Umayyad party and the various political forces opposed to it, while the doctrine of compulsion first grew in a different, Persian environment?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01178

And how could the limited personal influence of one individual—Maʿbad al-Juhanī’s supposed influence from Sansawayh—turn into a broad intellectual movement that rapidly spread among people from many social groups outside the ruling class, including religious scholars in a conservative region such as the Hijaz?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01179
If that personal influence really occurred, how could it grow into such a wide and powerful intellectual phenomenon unless another factor—social or political—helped produce that transformation?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01179
Five Pieces of Historical Evidence
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01180
Early historians and later researchers give us historical material that can shed a great deal of light on all these questions.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01181
This material allows us to reach a more realistic understanding of the problem than the one usually found in the studies available to us.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01182

We call these “historical materials” because the historians and researchers who recorded them generally treated them simply as pieces of information. They did not use them to build a broader interpretation beyond the historical narrative itself.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01183
We will now present five of these pieces of evidence, one by one and without comment. After that, we will draw the conclusions that we believe follow from them.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01184
1. Historians tell us that Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01185
“Abū Saʿīd, these kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth, and then they say, ‘Our actions happen only by the decree of God Most High.’”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01186
Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī replied:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01187
“The enemies of God are lying.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01188
He meant the Umayyads.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01189
2. Ibn Saʿd reports from Ayyūb al-Sakhtiyānī, a Basran who strongly opposed the Qadarites, that he argued with al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī more than once about the question of divine decree.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01190
Al-Ḥasan did not change his position until Ayyūb threatened him with the Umayyads. Only then did al-Ḥasan stop speaking in this way.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01191
Maʿbad al-Juhanī, as is well known, was a student of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01192
3. Al-Shahrastānī says:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01193

“…I saw a letter attributed to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī which he wrote to ʿAbd al-Malik ibn Marwān after the caliph asked him about free choice and compulsion. In it, he gave an answer consistent with Qadarite doctrine, supporting it with verses from the Qurʾān and arguments from reason. Perhaps the letter was really written by Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, since al-Ḥasan was not someone who would disagree with the early authorities on the principle that divine decree, both good and bad, comes from God Most High. These words were almost universally accepted among them.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01194
4. Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Murtaḍā gives us a fascinating account of Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01195
After Maʿbad, Ghaylān was the second major early figure to develop Qadarite thought into a more complete doctrine and theory.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01196

According to Ibn al-Murtaḍā, Ghaylān wrote to the Umayyad caliph ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz, calling on him to accept Qadarite doctrine. In the letter, he described the condition of Islam and the Muslims under Umayyad rule and the damage that had been done, to the point that:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01197
“The learned man is frightened into silence, while the ignorant man is not allowed to ask.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01198
The account suggests that ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz was not convinced by Ghaylān’s doctrine. Even so, he summoned him because he trusted his integrity and the sincerity of his religion.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01199
When Ghaylān arrived, the caliph asked him to help reform the affairs of the Muslims.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01200
Ghaylān agreed, on the condition that he be allowed to sell the treasures accumulated by the Umayyads and return people’s rights to their rightful owners. The caliph accepted.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01201
When Ghaylān took charge of the sale, he called out to the people of Damascus:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01202
“Come to the possessions of the traitors!”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01203
meaning the Umayyad rulers who had come before ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01204
“Come to the possessions of the oppressors! Come to the possessions of those who succeeded the Messenger among his community but did not follow his way or conduct!”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01205
As he sold the Umayyad possessions, he said to the crowd around him:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01206
“What can I say to those who claim that these men were rightly guided leaders, when this is what they owned while people were dying of hunger?”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01207
Ghaylān meant that the Umayyad rulers had enjoyed enormously valuable possessions while ordinary people were starving.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01208
According to the account, Hishām ibn ʿAbd al-Malik passed by while Ghaylān was speaking in this way.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01208
Hishām said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01209
“This man is insulting me and my fathers. By God, if I ever get hold of him, I will cut off his hands and feet.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01210
Later, when Hishām became the Umayyad caliph, Ghaylān fled to Armenia. From there he continued spreading reports of Hishām’s faults and of the injustice committed by Hishām and the Umayyads.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01211
The Umayyads, he argued, claimed that they ruled by God’s decree and destiny and that no one could escape that decree.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01212
Hishām ordered Ghaylān and his companion Ṣāliḥ to be brought before him. After keeping them imprisoned for several days, he ordered their hands and feet to be cut off.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01213
Ṣāliḥ died before Ghaylān.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01214
Ghaylān then turned to the people and said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01215

“May God destroy them”—meaning the Umayyads—“How many rights they have put to death! How much falsehood they have brought to life! How many people despised in God’s religion they have raised up, and how many people honored in God’s religion they have humiliated!”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01216
The Umayyads who heard him became angry and went to Hishām.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01216
They said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01217
“You cut off Ghaylān’s hands and feet, but you left his tongue free. He has made the people weep and awakened them to things they had not noticed before. Send someone to cut out his tongue.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01217
Hishām did so.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01218
Ghaylān died as a martyr to his defense of the rights of the oppressed and to his belief in human freedom.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01219
5. Historical works mention a third important figure who raised the banner of Qadarite doctrine and died for it: ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01220
According to the historical account, he was the first person to preach Qadarite doctrine openly in Damascus, before Ghaylān al-Dimashqī.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01221
He was also the teacher of Muʿāwiya II—Muʿāwiya ibn Yazīd ibn Muʿāwiya I, the founder of the Umayyad dynasty.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01222
ʿAmr influenced his student so strongly that Muʿāwiya II became a Qadarite like his teacher.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01223

When his father Yazīd died and the Umayyads wanted to pledge allegiance to Muʿāwiya as his successor, following the hereditary system created by his grandfather Muʿāwiya I, the young man consulted his teacher ʿAmr.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01224
ʿAmr advised him:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01225
“Either rule justly, or step down.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01226
Muʿāwiya II then considered his position.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01227
How could he choose? And if he remained caliph, how could he rule justly?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01228
He concluded that he would not be able to achieve the justice his teacher required of him.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01229
So he decided to step down from the caliphate.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01230
He announced his decision in a speech to the people of Damascus:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01231

“We have been tested through you, and you have been tested through us. My grandfather Muʿāwiya fought over authority with someone who had a greater right and stronger claim to it”—meaning ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib—“and he took upon himself what you know. He has now gone to meet the consequences of what he did.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01232
“Then my father Yazīd inherited it, though he was not worthy of it. He followed his own desires and thought his errors were right.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01233
“I do not wish to meet God carrying responsibility for you. So your affair is now yours. Give it to whomever you wish.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01234
“By God, if the caliphate is a prize, our family has already received its share. And if it is an evil, then the family of Abū Sufyān has already had enough of it.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01235
Historians say that after giving this speech and giving up the caliphate, Muʿāwiya II withdrew from public life.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01236
He died forty days later.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01237
The Umayyads then seized ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ and told him:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01238
“You corrupted him. You taught him this.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01239
They buried ʿAmr alive.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01240

He died for his Qadarite doctrine, which stood against an Umayyad system that claimed to rule in the name of divine right—that is, in the name of God’s decree and destiny, or the doctrine of compulsion, as the Umayyads presented it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival

What We Can Learn from These Five Pieces of Evidence
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01241
These are five examples of the “historical materials” given to us by early historians and later researchers.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01242
Yet they usually pass over them without trying to use them to uncover the social and political roots of the problem of human freedom and divine decree.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01243

Maʿbad al-Juhanī and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī raised the question in Iraq. Ghaylān al-Dimashqī and ʿAmr al-Maqṣūṣ raised it in Damascus. From there, the question helped set Arab thought as a whole moving further along the road toward philosophical thinking.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01244

Now that we have presented these examples in their bare historical form, we can ask what objective connection existed between them and the social and political conditions that gave them their historical meaning.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01245
We will examine them in the same order.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01245
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01246
Was it simply a coincidence that Maʿbad al-Juhanī and his companion ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī and said:
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01247
“Abū Saʿīd, these kings shed Muslim blood and take Muslim wealth, and then they say, ‘Our actions happen only by the decree of God Most High’”?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01247
Of course not.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01248
There was nothing accidental about it.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01249
Maʿbad al-Juhanī and ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār came to al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī complaining about and protesting against “these kings.”
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01250
Who were “these kings”?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01251
They were the rulers of the Muslims themselves: the Umayyad rulers. At that time, Muslims had no other kings.
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01252
What were Maʿbad and ʿAṭāʾ protesting against?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01253
What exactly were they complaining about?
Intellectual Conflict and the Foundations of Cultural Revival
passage-en-01254
The historical evidence is perfectly clear. It answers the question without any need for interpretation.
